Predicting the top-level ontological concepts of domain entities using word
embeddings, informal definitions, and deep learning
Alcides Gonçalves Lopes Junior ∗, Joel Luis Carbonera, Daniela Schimidt, Mara Abel
Institute of Informatics, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
A R T I C L E
I N F O
Keywords:
Ontology learning
Deep learning
Well-founded ontology
A B S T R A C T
Ontology development is a challenging task that encompasses many time-consuming activities. One of these
activities is the classification of the domain entities (concepts and instances) according to top-level concepts.
This activity is usually performed manually by an ontology engineer. However, when the set of entities
increases in size, associating each entity to the proper top-level ontological concept becomes challenging and
requires a high level of expertise in both the target domain and ontology engineering. This paper proposes a
deep learning approach that automatically classifies domain entities into top-level concepts using their informal
definitions and the word embedding of the terms that represent them. From these inputs, we feed a deep
neural network consisting of two modules: a feed-forward neural network and a bi-directional recurrent neural
network with long short-term units. Our architecture combines both outputs of these modules into a dense
layer and provides the probabilities of each candidate class. For validating our proposal, we have developed a
dataset based on the OntoWordNet ontology, which provides a classification of WordNet synsets into concepts
specified by DOLCE-lite-plus top-level ontology. Our experiments show that our proposal outperforms the
baseline approaches by 6% regarding the F-score. In addition, our proposal is less affected by the polysemy in
the terms that represent the domain entities than the compared approaches. Consequently, our proposal can
consider more instances during its training than the baseline methods.

Introduction Ontologies have proved useful in many domains ( Abel, Perrin, Car- bonera, & Garcia , 0000 ; Arp, Smith, & Spear , 2015 ; Garcia, Graciolli, De Ros, & Abel , 2017 ) and play a crucial role in the semantic web ( Gangemi, Guarino, Masolo, Oltramari, & Schneider , 2002 ; Khadir, Aliane, & Guessoum , 2021 ). According to Studer, Benjamins, and Fensel ( 1998 ), an ontology is a formal and explicit specification of a shared conceptualization, where: conceptualization refers to an abstract model constituted by the concepts identified from phenomena in the world; explicit means that the types of concepts used and the constraints on their use are explicitly defined; formal refers to the fact that the ontology should be machine-readable; shared reflects the consensual knowledge accepted by the communities which the ontology should capture. In general, an ontology provides a set of concepts, relations, properties, and axioms that represent the ontological nature of the entities. The domain ontologies developed based on top-level ontologies have the advantage of adhering to a philosophically well-founded meaning. This strategy provides a more uniform view over the domain and, potentially, can help further alignment with other ontologies developed under the same top-level ontology. In the proposed dataset, we create an instance for each label of an OntoWordNet entity. For example, as presented in Table 1 , both labels ‘‘rock’’ and ‘‘stone’’ name the same entity in the OntoWordNet ontology. However, we created two different instances in our dataset because ‘‘rock’’ and ‘‘stone’’ probably have different word embeddings vectors. By applying this strategy to the other OntoWordNet entities, we increase the dataset size and account for the variations of each entity’s labels. Thus, from the 86,982 entities of the OntoWordNet ontology, we create 147,626 instances in our dataset. As presented in Fig. 1 , the DLP contains a hierarchy of concepts organized through ‘‘is-a’’ relationships (e.g., the Physical Object is an Endurant), the class of one dataset instance can be any of the DLP super concepts that generalize the domain entity. For example, the instance represented by the entity label ‘‘rock’’ can have as target class Functional Matter, Physical Object, or Endurant. In order to deal with this characteristic of the ontologies, we created two versions of our dataset. In the first version, we have used the direct super-class in DOLCE of the dataset instance (e.g., Functional-Matter, Activity, etc.) as the target class (as presented in Dataset 1 of Table 1 ). In the second version, we have used the most generic top-level concept of DLP (below the concept of ‘‘Thing’’, which is not informative) that classifies the instance as the target class (e.g., Endurant, Perdurant, Quality, Abstract, etc, as presented in Dataset 2 of Table 1 ). We can generate other classes with different levels of generality, but this is not the focus of this work. 3.2. Proposed deep neural network architecture Another contribution of this work is the deep neural network ar- chitecture for classifying domain entities into top-level ontology con- cepts. This architecture combines the outputs of two neural network modules trained together: a feed-forward neural network (FNN) and a bi-directional recurrent neural network with long short-term units (BLSTM). Fig. 2 depicts the architecture of the deep neural network. We have used a feed-forward neural network because of its performance on classification based on word vectors. Also, we have used a (BLSTM) because of its performance on learning better suitable features from free-text inputs ( Lamurias et al. , 2019 ; Otter, Medina, & Kalita , 2020 ; Qiu et al. , 2020 ). Thus, in order to apply our approach, it is necessary to combine the dataset described in Section 3.1 with a pre-trained word embedding model. The top part of Fig. 2 describes how we initialized the deep neural network using an instance of the dataset proposed in Section 3.1 .
